text.p: Gold prices fell again and world copper prices dropped sharply on Wednesday on signs of a buildup in stocks and production of the metal just as demand makes its seasonal decline in the U.S. and European summer.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, Chicago wheat prices rose on talk of potential Middle East imports.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower across the board Wednesday on moderate volumes, after Tuesday's shortcovering bounce ran into more trade selling in gold and silver, traders said. COMEX August gold ended down $2.10 at $318.90 an ounce, after recovering from a morning low at $316.20 to a session high at $321.30. The COMEX August/December spread narrowed to $3.60 an ounce Wednesday, from $5.60 six weeks ago. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $318.00/50, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $317.30, the London Wednesday morning fix at $315.75, and the New York close Tuesday around $319.80/30. "Gold opened lower in the U.S. after more trade selling in Europe, then recovered on some shortcovering, but didn't get above yesterdays high, so it's still not a very good performance, especially when you consider some of the buying this week has been funds rolling short positions into the December contract," said Scott Mehlman, chief bullion dealer at Credit Lyonnais Rouse in

Copper prices turned sharply lower during late LME Wednesday ring and kerb trading, with the market ending weak and near 4-1/2 month lows. Traders said a mid-afternoon spell of consolidation in the $2,260s proved to be illusory, when the market buckled under a renewed bout of speculative liquidation. This took prices conclusively under $2,240/45 support, and established $2,200 as an initial downside objective. Analysts said sentiment has become increasingly sour in recent sessions, with metal stocks rising and demand slowing down for summer. Final three months trade was at $2,236, a hefty $132 down from Tuesday's kerb after the deluge of investment fund sales, long liquidation, and option-related sales of the last 24 hours. Since mid-June, when copper peaked for the year at $2,609 a tonne, prices have shed some 14 percent, and the decline has further to go, traders said.
Elsewhere, metal prices wobbled, but once an initial mark-down with copper was not translated into similar selling some stabilised.

Aluminium climbed away from a potential test of sell-stops near $1,530/40, and clawed its way back up to $1,568, up $3 from Tuesday. Traders said the market is not really responding to the string of inventory drawdowns, although there has not been heavy selling pressure.
Lead and zinc both flipped back up into the plus column, closing at $650 and $1,462, up $1 and $3 respectively.
But tin and nickel lost ground. Tin closed $30 lower at $5,510, and is now seen re-testing 2-1/4 year lows of $5,490.

Nickel was only partially cushioned by the Falconbridge strike vote ahead of the labour contract expiry later this month. It finished $45 easier at $6,890, reflecting rising stocks and talk of ample Russian availability.
Alloy was marked down, and closed some $12 easier at $1,415/20 a tonne.

Fund short covering amid signals the market was oversold and talk Egypt was seeking U.S. wheat boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to a higher close, traders said. Another strong rally in nearby soybeans contributed to advances in the wheat pit as did rain in portions of the U.S. Midwest which was slowing harvest of the winter wheat crop. Also traders said there was a rumour that Egypt was seeking 750,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for September/October shipment. CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed 7-1/4 to 9-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with July up 9-1/4 at $3.25-3/4. September was up 9-1/2 at $3.34-1/4.

NYMEX oil prices ended lower Wednesday on bearish oil inventory data and on news that Iraq took another step toward resuming oil sales. August crude settled 27 cents a barrel lower at $19.46. August heating oil finished 0.35 cent a gallon lower at 52.65 cents while August gasoline ended 0.69 cent a gallon lower at 58.23 cents. "Oil supplies are plentiful, and there is certainly more than enough gasoline supply to meet demand this summer. The report was bearish," said Allendale Inc trader James Cordier of weekly oil inventory released by the American Petroleum Institute (API) on Tuesday evening.
